repulse

/rih-PULS/ - the stress falls on PULS · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Repulse means to drive back an attack or advance, forcing it to retreat.

Guard bees massed at the hive entrance and repulsed the hornet three times before it finally gave up.

Example

For eighty years the mountain's north ridge repulsed everyone who tried it. Storms turned parties around at the shoulder; ice sheeted the one workable chimney; a rope team in 1963 got within four hundred feet and was driven down by wind that peeled a tent from its anchors. The ridge did not care how good anyone was. It sent them all back down.

Repulse is the exact word for what the ridge did, because it means to drive back, to repel an attack or advance — the push comes on, and force sends it back the way it came. Resist would only say the mountain held; repulse says the climbers ended up back where they started.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

repel: To repel is the near-twin with a wider day job — a magnet repels its match, spray repels insects, and no battle is required anywhere. Repulse is the sharper military word: it wants an actual attack or advance in the sentence, coming on and being driven back.

beat back: Beat back is the plain, everyday phrase for turning back an advancing force in a real struggle — firefighters beat back flames, defenders beat back a charge. Repulse says the same thing in formal military register: the historian's word for an assault driven off.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

welcome: open the gates to what approaches

give way: break, and let the advance pour through

Where it sits · how decisively the attack is beaten

resist → repulse → crush

resist vs. repulse: Resist is milder than repulse — the line strains and holds its ground, the outcome undecided — while repulse sends the attack back the way it came.

crush vs. repulse: Crush goes further than repulse — a repulsed force retreats in order and may try again, while a crushed one is finished as a force at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-: back

Root — pulse: pushed, driven (Latin pellere, pulsus)

Put it together: Re- (back) + pulse (pushed, driven) = pushed back. Latin repellere, repulsus is force answered with force: the advance comes on, and the defenders drive it back the way it came. The same puls- beats inside pulse itself — blood driven through in pushes — and inside propulsion, the forward version of this backward shove.

Use the root in a new word: propulsion: The rocket's propulsion cut out ninety seconds after launch, and the control room went silent.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / martial

Repulse is the battlefield verb: an advance comes on and is driven back — armies, raids, surges, takeover bids. Repel is its near-twin with a wider day job (fabrics repel water; spray repels insects); when the sentence contains an attack, repulse hits harder. It also has a second life — 'his table manners repulsed her' — but this unit's sense is the military one. Among the unit's disapproval words, repudiate rejects claims and reprove corrects people; repulse alone stops a charge.
